chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from more than one of our companions, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who has a concubine, and his wife annoys him and is jealous of her, so he says to her, 'She is a charity (gift) upon you.' He (the Imam) said: If he dedicated her to Allah and mentioned Allah's name, he is not permitted to have sexual relations with her. And if he did not mention Allah's name, she remains his concubine, and he does with her as he pleases.

The correct interpretation of this report is that we construe it in one of two ways: First, that it is obligatory for him to fulfill it if he made it a valid vow (nadhr), and there is no religious or worldly benefit for him in breaking it; and it is permissible for him to break it only if he derives benefit and advantage from it, as we stated regarding oaths. The second way is that we construe it as recommended (mustahabb).
ai.seo_question: What is the legal effect when a husband declares his concubine a charity to his wife?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* elucidates the juristic nuances of declaring a concubine *sadaqah* (charity) to a wife, distinguishing between a vow dedicated to Allah which restricts conjugal rights, and a non-dedicated declaration which does not. Shia scholars interpret this through two primary lenses: either as a binding *nadhr* (vow) where the man must fulfill the spiritual intent, or as a recommended act (*mustahabb*) where flexibility remains. This reflects the broader Shia legal principle of balancing literal textual interpretation with the underlying intent (*niyyah*) and practical benefit (*maslaha*).
